title: Preventing and Managing Non-infectious Disease
subtitle: Prevention levels, evaluating a prevention campaign, and judging treatments by effectiveness, cost and access
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: use secondary sources to evaluate the effectiveness of current disease-prevention methods and develop strategies for the prevention of a non-infectious disease, including but not limited to: educational programs and campaigns
investigate the treatment/management, and possible future directions for further research, of a non-infectious disease using an example from one of the non-infectious diseases categories listed above
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate the effectiveness of a campaign to prevent a non-infectious disease
inquiryQuestion: How can non-infectious diseases be prevented?
lessonIntent: Students can classify prevention as primary, secondary or tertiary, evaluate the effectiveness of a prevention campaign such as SunSmart using secondary data, and evaluate a treatment by weighing effectiveness, cost and accessibility.
examSkill: Evaluate a named prevention campaign against clear criteria and evidence, and explain why the most effective treatment is not always the most appropriate for a given patient.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, preventing and managing non-infectious disease. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Preventing and Managing Non-infectious Disease (Year 12 Biology, Module 8, Lesson 15)

scenes.heading: Slip, slop, slap
scenes.body: In 1981 a cartoon seagull told Australians to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. Did it actually prevent cancer?
scenes.callout: How do you prove a campaign prevented a disease?
scenes.caption: Slip Slop Slap launched in 1981; melanoma rates in younger Australians have since fallen.

voiceover.text: In nineteen eighty one, a cartoon seagull named Sid appeared on Australian television, singing that everyone should slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. It became one of the best known health campaigns in the world, and it grew into the SunSmart program. Australia has one of the highest skin cancer rates on Earth, so the stakes were high. Decades later, melanoma rates in younger Australians have been falling. But here's the tricky part. How do you prove a campaign caused that, rather than something else? That's the skill for today, evaluating prevention, alongside how we judge the treatments used once disease has developed.

scenes.heading: Three levels of prevention
scenes.body: Prevention is classified by when it acts along the disease timeline, before, early, or after the disease is established.

bullets.text: Primary prevention stops disease before it starts, like vaccination or healthy eating.
Secondary prevention catches disease early through screening, like mammograms.
Tertiary prevention manages established disease to limit complications, like cardiac rehab.

scenes.secondary: The key is timing relative to the disease. Primary acts before any disease exists, secondary acts when the disease is present but silent, and tertiary acts once symptoms and damage have begun.
scenes.callout: Before it starts, catch it early, limit the damage.
scenes.caption: Primary prevention acts before disease, secondary detects it early, tertiary manages established disease.

voiceover.text: Let's start with the three levels of prevention, because students mix them up constantly. The trick is timing relative to the disease. Primary prevention happens before any disease exists, and its job is to stop it developing. Vaccination, healthy eating, quitting smoking and campaigns like SunSmart are all primary. Secondary prevention happens once the disease is present but still silent, and its job is early detection through screening, like mammograms, bowel cancer screening and skin checks. Tertiary prevention happens after the disease is established, and its job is to manage it, prevent complications and improve quality of life, like cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack. So ask yourself, is this acting before the disease, catching it early, or managing it once it's here?

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Three more terms frame how we judge prevention and treatment.

bullets.text: Health promotion campaign: a coordinated program using media and education to change behaviour.
Social determinants of health: non-medical factors like income, education and housing.
Cost-effectiveness: the health outcome gained for each dollar spent.

scenes.callout: Change behaviour, mind the social factors, count the dollars.
scenes.caption: Health promotion campaign, social determinants of health, cost-effectiveness.

voiceover.text: Three more terms before we evaluate anything. A health promotion campaign is a coordinated program that uses media, education and often policy to change people's behaviour and reduce a risk factor. Social determinants of health are the non medical factors, like income, education, housing and access to healthcare, that strongly shape disease risk and outcomes. And cost effectiveness is the health outcome gained for each dollar spent, which is how governments decide where to put limited money.

scenes.heading: How to evaluate a prevention campaign
scenes.body: A campaign works only if it changes behaviour and that change lowers disease, so evaluate each link in the chain.

bullets.text: Reach and awareness: did the target audience see and remember the message?
Behaviour change: did people actually change, e.g. less sunburn, more hats and sunscreen?
Health outcomes: did incidence or mortality fall, allowing for time lags?
Attribution and cost: could other factors explain it, and was it worth the money?

scenes.secondary: Cancers can take decades to develop after exposure, so outcome data lag behind behaviour change. Screening changes can also raise recorded incidence even when true risk falls.
scenes.callout: Awareness, behaviour, outcome, then ask: was it really the campaign?
scenes.caption: Evaluate a campaign on reach, behaviour change, health outcomes, attribution and cost.

voiceover.text: So how do you evaluate a campaign? Think of it as a chain, and test every link. First, reach and awareness. Did the target audience actually see the message and remember it? Second, behaviour change. Awareness is worthless unless people change what they do, so look for survey data, like fewer people getting sunburnt, and more wearing hats and sunscreen. Third, health outcomes. Did the incidence or mortality of the disease actually fall? Be careful, because cancers can take decades to develop, so outcome data lag well behind behaviour. Fourth, attribution and cost. Could something else explain the change, like new laws, better screening or an ageing population? And was the result worth the money spent? A strong evaluation checks all four links, using data, before reaching a judgement.

scenes.heading: Evaluate SunSmart
scenes.question: Using secondary sources, evaluate the effectiveness of the SunSmart (Slip Slop Slap) campaign in preventing skin cancer in Australia.
scenes.coachNote: Work through the chain: reach, behaviour, outcome, then attribution and cost, and finish with a clear judgement.
steps: Reach: very high; the slogan is recognised by most Australians and is taught in schools.
Behaviour: surveys since the 1980s show more hat, shade and sunscreen use and less sunburn.
Outcome: melanoma incidence in younger Australians has fallen since the 1990s, while older age groups, exposed before the campaign, still rise.
Attribution: other measures helped too, like shade in schools and solarium bans, so the campaign is one part of a wider strategy.
Judgement: highly effective as part of a combined strategy, with falling rates in the generations who grew up with it ✓
scenes.caption: SunSmart: high reach, better sun protection, falling melanoma in younger Australians; effective as part of a wider strategy.

voiceover.text: Let's evaluate SunSmart, using the chain. Reach first. It's extremely high, because the slogan is known by most Australians and sun safety is built into schools, with no hat, no play rules. Behaviour next. Surveys since the nineteen eighties show more people using hats, shade and sunscreen, and fewer getting sunburnt. Now the outcome. Melanoma incidence in younger Australians, the generations who grew up with the campaign, has been falling since the nineteen nineties, while rates in older people, who were exposed before it began, have kept rising. That pattern is exactly what you'd expect if the campaign worked, given the long lag. But attribution matters. Other measures helped as well, like shade in schools and bans on commercial solariums, so the campaign is one part of a wider strategy. So the judgement is that SunSmart has been highly effective, as part of a combined approach, and economic studies suggest it saves more than it costs.

scenes.heading: How to evaluate a treatment
scenes.body: Once disease has developed, evaluating a treatment means weighing how well it works, what it costs, and who can actually get it.

bullets.text: Effectiveness: how much it reduces the disease, backed by the strength of the evidence.
Cost: the price before and after subsidies like the PBS and Medicare.
Accessibility: geography, income, time and health literacy decide who can use it.

scenes.secondary: These pull against each other, and unequal access is called health inequity. The most effective treatment on paper is not always the most appropriate for a real patient.
scenes.callout: Effectiveness, cost, access. Weigh all three, don't just list.
scenes.caption: Evaluate a treatment by balancing effectiveness, cost and accessibility, not by listing features.

voiceover.text: Now to treatment, once a non infectious disease has developed. To evaluate a treatment, you weigh three things together. First, effectiveness, how much it reduces the disease and how strong the evidence is. Statins, for example, cut major heart attacks and strokes by about a quarter in large randomised trials. Second, cost, before and after subsidies. In Australia, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme subsidises approved medicines, so a drug costing tens of thousands of dollars a year can cost a patient a small co payment, and Medicare covers hospital care. Third, accessibility, which is never purely financial. People in rural and remote areas have less access to specialists and rehabilitation, and income and health literacy shape who gets treated, which is called health inequity. These three pull against each other, so the most effective treatment isn't always the most appropriate.

rows: Cuts major events by about a quarter
Cheap on the PBS, widely available
Cheap on the PBS, very accessible

scenes.heading: Choosing Marcus's treatment
scenes.question: Marcus, 48, has early-stage type 2 diabetes with a fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L. He is overweight and works long hours with little time to cook or exercise. What treatment approach fits best, and why isn't it simply the most powerful drug?
scenes.coachNote: Match the treatment to the disease stage first, then weigh effectiveness against what Marcus can realistically sustain.
steps: His diabetes is early-stage, so guidelines recommend lifestyle intervention as first-line treatment, not a drug.
Diet, exercise and 5 to 10 percent weight loss directly reduce his insulin resistance, the root driver.
If lifestyle alone doesn't reach his target after a few months, add metformin, which is cheap on the PBS.
His long hours make lifestyle change hard to sustain, so Medicare-funded dietitian and diabetes-educator support improves adherence.
Answer: lifestyle first, then metformin if needed; the best treatment is the effective one Marcus can actually maintain ✓
scenes.caption: Early T2D: lifestyle first-line, then metformin; the appropriate choice fits the patient, not just the biology.

voiceover.text: Let's apply this to a patient. Marcus is forty eight, with early type 2 diabetes and a fasting glucose of eight point two. He's overweight, and works long hours with little time to cook or exercise. What treatment fits best, and why isn't it just the strongest drug? Step one, match the treatment to the stage. His diabetes is early, so Australian guidelines recommend lifestyle change as the first line treatment. Step two, the mechanism. Diet, exercise and losing five to ten percent of body weight directly reduce his insulin resistance, so this targets the cause. Step three, escalate only if needed. If lifestyle alone doesn't reach his target within a few months, add metformin, which is cheap on the PBS. Step four, the human reality. His long hours make lifestyle change hard to sustain, so Medicare funded dietitian support helps him stick with it. The best treatment is the effective one he can actually keep up.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: assuming the most biologically effective treatment is always the most appropriate. Cost, access and patient circumstances decide appropriateness too.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: judging a campaign by awareness alone. Knowing a slogan is not the same as changing behaviour or lowering disease. Trap 3: thinking metformin restores the pancreas. It lowers glucose by reducing the liver's output and improving insulin sensitivity, so it manages rather than cures.
scenes.callout: Effective is not always appropriate, awareness is not outcome, metformin manages.
scenes.caption: Most effective is not most appropriate; awareness is not outcome; metformin manages, it does not cure.

voiceover.text: Three traps that quietly cost marks. Trap one, assuming the most biologically effective treatment is automatically the most appropriate. Bypass surgery may be the most effective option for severe heart disease, but for a frail elderly patient the surgical risk can outweigh the benefit. Appropriateness weighs effectiveness against cost, access, side effects and the individual. Trap two, judging a campaign by awareness alone. Everyone knowing the slogan doesn't prove anything unless behaviour changed and disease rates fell. Trap three, thinking metformin repairs the pancreas. It lowers blood glucose by reducing the liver's glucose output and improving insulin sensitivity, so if you stop taking it, glucose rises again. It manages the disease, it doesn't cure it.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary prevention: (a) an influenza vaccination; (b) a mammogram screening a woman with no symptoms; (c) a cardiac rehabilitation program after a heart attack; (d) a public campaign promoting sunscreen.
answerSteps: (a) Vaccination stops disease before it develops, so it is primary prevention.
(b) A mammogram detects disease early in someone without symptoms, so it is secondary prevention.
(c) Cardiac rehab manages established disease after an event, so it is tertiary prevention.
(d) A sunscreen campaign reduces a risk factor before disease, so it is primary prevention.
scenes.caption: (a) primary, (b) secondary, (c) tertiary, (d) primary.

voiceover.text: Quick check, sorting examples into the three prevention levels. Part a, an influenza vaccination. Part b, a mammogram screening a woman with no symptoms. Part c, a cardiac rehabilitation program after a heart attack. Part d, a public campaign promoting sunscreen. Pause and sort them. Right, ask each time whether it acts before the disease, catches it early, or manages it once it's here. Part a, vaccination stops disease before it develops, so it's primary. Part b, a mammogram in someone with no symptoms detects disease early, so it's secondary. Part c, cardiac rehab manages established disease, so it's tertiary. And part d, a sunscreen campaign reduces a risk factor before any disease, so it's primary again.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Primary prevention acts before disease, secondary detects it early, tertiary manages it once established.
Evaluate a campaign along the chain: reach, behaviour change, health outcomes, then attribution and cost.
SunSmart has been highly effective as part of a wider strategy, with falling melanoma in younger Australians.
Evaluate a treatment by weighing effectiveness, cost and accessibility; access in Australia is still unequal.
The most effective treatment is not always the most appropriate one for a given patient.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating prevention or treatment? Ask what changed, what the data show, what it costs, and who it reaches.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: prevention levels, the campaign chain, SunSmart, treatment criteria, appropriateness.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, primary prevention acts before disease, secondary detects it early, and tertiary manages it once it's established. Second, evaluate a campaign along the chain, reach, behaviour change and health outcomes, then ask whether something else could explain the result, and whether it was worth the cost. Third, SunSmart has been highly effective as part of a wider strategy, with melanoma falling in the younger Australians who grew up with it. Fourth, evaluate a treatment by weighing effectiveness, cost and accessibility, remembering that access in Australia is still unequal. And fifth, the most effective treatment is not always the most appropriate for a particular patient. See you next lesson.
